message: Select a card (1 more) to put on the bottom of your library
annotation_description: During the mulligan process (putting one card back from a 7-card hand to go to 6), GPT4om Sarge bottomed Orcish Bowmasters, one of the best cards in Modern and an excellent 2-drop that provides early interaction and board presence. The hand already has Necrodominance (which requires BBB and is hard to cast with only 1 Swamp), Sheoldred (4 mana, no way to cast soon), and March of Wretched Sorrow (situational). The hand lacks a second land entirely. Bottoming Bowmasters - a cheap, impactful card that could be played on turn 2 - instead of a more expensive or less castable card like Sheoldred, Necrodominance, or March of Wretched Sorrow is a significant error. With only one Swamp in hand, keeping the cheap interactive creatures is critical.

message: Select a card (1 more) to put on the bottom of your library
annotation_description: Weapons Manufacturing is the key engine card that turns all the cheap artifacts (Mishra's Bauble, Tormod's Crypt, Aether Spellbomb) into 2-damage Munitions tokens. Without it, the hand is just a collection of low-impact artifacts and an Arcbound Ravager with limited sacrifice fodder value. Tormod's Crypt is a narrow sideboard-quality card that does nothing against many decks and has no board impact on its own.

Castle Locthwain enters tapped when you don't control a Swamp. Since the player has no lands in play, Castle Locthwain will enter tapped and they cannot cast Thoughtseize or Inquisition of Kozilek on turn 1. If they had played Undercity Sewers instead, it also enters tapped but has the Island Swamp type, meaning on turn 2 they could play Castle Locthwain untapped (since they'd control a Swamp). By playing Castle Locthwain first, when they play Undercity Sewers on turn 2 they'll have both lands available, but the same is true in reverse. However, the key difference is that playing Undercity Sewers first gives a surveil 1 trigger, which is relevant for Psychic Frog (fueling the graveyard for the flying ability) and generally provides card selection. Castle Locthwain first provides no such advantage. The sequencing of Undercity Sewers first is slightly better due to the surveil value.

message: You may choose an alternative cost
chosen_display: Cast with alternative cost: Exile two black cards from your hand (source: <font color='#696969' object_id='6572e32f-6e99-4e1b-bf48-67535973d200'>Soul Spike</font> [657])
annotation_description: The player exiled Inquisition of Kozilek and Thoughtseize (their only two black cards in hand besides Psychic Frog) to cast Soul Spike for free on turn 1. This deals 4 damage to an opponent at 20 life and gains 4 life, which is nearly irrelevant this early. In exchange, they lose their two best disruption spells - Thoughtseize and Inquisition of Kozilek - which are premium hand disruption that could strip key cards from the opponent. They're left with just Undercity Sewers and Psychic Frog in hand, with no way to interact with the opponent's game plan. Trading two of the best cards in the deck for 4 damage when the opponent is at 20 life is a catastrophic value trade.

Casting Mishra's Bauble before playing Spirebluff Canal from hand. The player should play their land first (Spirebluff Canal enters untapped since they control only 1 other land), then cast their 0-cost artifacts. Playing the land first would allow them to cast Aether Spellbomb this turn as well, and potentially set up a better board for Arcbound Ravager next turn. Additionally, if they use Mishra's Bauble to look at their own library top card, they could surveil/plan better after seeing what's coming, but playing the land first is strictly better sequencing since it doesn't cost anything and opens up more options.

Tormod's Crypt is a free artifact that's fine to deploy, but the opponent only has Soul Spike in graveyard which isn't threatening. Meanwhile, Mishra's Bauble is on the battlefield untapped and should be activated first (sacrificing it to look at opponent's top card and draw next upkeep) before casting Tormod's Crypt. Bauble's sacrifice is pure upside and should be done as early as possible to get the delayed draw. Additionally, casting Aether Spellbomb (using Fiery Islet for the {1}) would be better sequencing since it's another artifact on board to help Improvise for Kappa Cannoneer, and Spirebluff Canal hasn't been played yet this turn as the land drop. The correct sequence would be: activate Mishra's Bauble first, then play Spirebluff Canal, then cast Aether Spellbomb, then cast Tormod's Crypt — maximizing artifacts on board for future Improvise and getting the Bauble draw triggered.

Mishra's Bauble is a free activation that lets you look at the top card of the opponent's library and draw a card next upkeep. There is no downside to activating it — the information is about the opponent's top card, not yours. With Tormod's Crypt entering the battlefield and Arcbound Ravager in hand (which benefits from having artifacts to sacrifice), cracking the Bauble now would also put it in the graveyard for potential graveyard-based interactions and get a free card draw next turn. The reasoning given ('forces opponent to see our top card') is factually wrong — Bauble lets YOU look at TARGET PLAYER's library top card. Declining a free cantrip with no downside is a clear mistake.

chosen_display: Fiery Islet — {1}, {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Draw a card. [Activate]
annotation_description: Sacrificing Fiery Islet to draw a card during combat on Turn 1 is very costly. Fiery Islet is one of only two lands available (the other being Spirebluff Canal in hand), and sacrificing it means going down to zero lands on board with only one land in hand. This severely delays casting Arcbound Ravager (needs 2 mana) and especially Kappa Cannoneer. Additionally, each artifact on board helps cast Kappa Cannoneer via Improvise, and Fiery Islet could have been tapped for mana toward future plays. The player also has Mishra's Bauble available as a free draw (delayed), which would accomplish card draw without destroying a land. Using Mishra's Bauble first for the draw effect would have been far better sequencing.

Mishra's Bauble is a free activation that lets you look at the top card of the opponent's library and draw a card next upkeep. There is no downside to activating it, and it provides information and card advantage. Additionally, sacrificing it now means it will be in the graveyard, which could be relevant for future plays. Tormod's Crypt could also be activated to exile the opponent's graveyard (which contains Soul Spike), though that's less critical. But declining Mishra's Bauble activation is leaving free value on the table.

chosen_display: Tormod's Crypt — {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Exile target player's grav... [Activate]
annotation_description: Using Tormod's Crypt to exile the opponent's graveyard containing only a single Soul Spike. While Soul Spike in the graveyard could theoretically matter for delve or other graveyard synergies, in a typical Modern deck with Castle Locthwain, there's unlikely to be significant graveyard interaction worth sacrificing the Crypt for right now. Meanwhile, Tormod's Crypt is an artifact that could be kept on the battlefield to feed Arcbound Ravager (sacrifice for counters), help cast Kappa Cannoneer via Improvise, and trigger Kappa Cannoneer's ETB/artifact-enters ability. The Crypt also serves as ongoing graveyard hate pressure. Sacrificing it now for minimal value when it could provide more utility later seems premature.

chosen_display: Mishra's Bauble — {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Look at the top card of ta... [Activate]
annotation_description: Mishra's Bauble was used to look at Qwen3L ESPN's own library instead of the opponent's. Looking at the opponent's top card provides strictly more useful information — you already know your own deck composition and can't act on knowing your own top card in most cases, whereas knowing the opponent's top card helps inform sequencing and threat assessment. The draw-a-card trigger happens regardless of the target chosen.

Casting Mishra's Bauble before playing a land is suboptimal. Qwen3L ESPN has Spirebluff Canal and Urza's Saga in hand. Playing Urza's Saga first is important because Urza's Saga is a key card that starts generating construct tokens and can tutor artifacts. Playing the land costs nothing and doesn't prevent casting Mishra's Bauble afterward (Bauble costs 0). Additionally, casting Mishra's Bauble from hand before playing a land means the opponent sees the Bauble on the stack and gets information. More importantly, with Arcbound Ravager in hand, playing Urza's Saga this turn sets up the saga counter progression. The Bauble can still be cast after the land drop since it costs 0 mana.

Qwen3L ESPN chose to cast Aether Spellbomb using the colorless mana from Urza's Saga (Chapter I) instead of activating Mishra's Bauble first. Mishra's Bauble is a free activation that sacrifices itself to look at the top card of the opponent's library and draw a card next upkeep. Since the Bauble requires tapping and sacrificing, and there's no reason to hold it, activating it first would have been strictly better sequencing. More importantly, with Urza's Saga on the battlefield, each artifact in play matters for potential Construct token size (Chapter II) and for Arcbound Ravager fodder. However, Mishra's Bauble was going to be sacrificed anyway for its effect, so the key issue is information: activating Bauble first gives you a look at the opponent's top card before committing to your main phase plays. Additionally, casting Aether Spellbomb before activating Bauble means the Spellbomb enters and could have been counted as an artifact entering for Kappa Cannoneer triggers later, but Kappa Cannoneer isn't in play yet. The sequencing error is minor — activating Mishra's Bauble first costs nothing and provides information, and should have been done before spending mana.

With only two lands (Castle Locthwain and Undercity Sewers producing B and U/B), casting Emperor of Bones over Psychic Frog is questionable. Psychic Frog is a stronger card in this matchup - it provides card advantage on combat damage, can grow via discard, and gains evasion. Emperor of Bones needs graveyard targets to get real value from its adapt ability, and the opponent's graveyard currently only has Tormod's Crypt and Mishra's Bauble (no creatures to reanimate). Additionally, the opponent has Aether Spellbomb on board which can bounce either creature for just {U}, and Emperor of Bones is more vulnerable to this since it needs to accumulate value over time. Psychic Frog at least threatens immediate card draw if it connects and can be pumped. Orcish Bowmasters could also be considered since it has flash and could be held to punish the opponent's Mishra's Bauble delayed draw trigger, but casting it main phase would still get the ETB ping.

chosen_display: Mishra's Bauble — {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Look at the top card of ta... [Activate]
annotation_description: Chose to look at own library with Mishra's Bauble instead of the opponent's. Looking at the opponent's top card is generally more valuable since you'll see your own card when you draw it, while knowing the opponent's upcoming draw helps inform strategic decisions.

message: Select up to one card from a graveyard
annotation_description: Emperor of Bones exiles a card from a graveyard and can later reanimate creature cards exiled with it when +1/+1 counters are placed on it (via adapt). Soul Spike is an instant, not a creature card, so it can never be reanimated by Emperor of Bones. The opponent's graveyard contained Tormod's Crypt and two Mishra's Baubles — none of which are creatures either, but exiling Tormod's Crypt would have been more strategically valuable since it removes the opponent's ability to recur or use it (it's already on the battlefield though, so this is moot). However, exiling Soul Spike from your own graveyard is purely wasteful — it removes a card that could potentially be exiled for other graveyard-matters effects, and gains nothing since Emperor of Bones can only put creature cards onto the battlefield. Any of the opponent's graveyard cards (especially Tormod's Crypt to deny potential recursion synergies) would have been slightly better targets, or simply declining the trigger altogether would preserve Soul Spike in the graveyard for potential Psychic Frog's exile-three-cards ability.

chosen_display: Fiery Islet — {1}, {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Draw a card. [Activate]
annotation_description: Sacrificing Fiery Islet to draw a card is costly here. Qwen3L ESPN has Arcbound Ravager and Kappa Cannoneer in hand - both require mana to cast. Fiery Islet is one of only two lands (alongside Urza's Saga which will be sacrificed after chapter III). Losing the land sets back the ability to cast Arcbound Ravager (needs 2 mana) and especially Kappa Cannoneer (needs 6 mana, reduced by improvise). Additionally, Urza's Saga is on chapter II and will need to be sacrificed after chapter III, meaning land drops are critical. The player also has Spirebluff Canal in hand which they haven't played yet, but even with that they'd only have 2 lands total. Meanwhile, Aether Spellbomb could have been sacrificed for {1} to draw a card instead, preserving the land while still getting a draw, and Aether Spellbomb is less valuable as a permanent since the opponent's only creature (Emperor of Bones) is not a high-priority bounce target compared to needing mana development. Furthermore, sacrificing Fiery Islet reduces artifact count, which matters for Urza's Saga construct tokens and Kappa Cannoneer's improvise.

Orcish Bowmasters has flash and is typically better held to cast on the opponent's turn to punish card draws and react to threats. Playing it in the precombat main phase wastes the flash advantage. Psychic Frog is the better proactive play here since it wants to attack and connect for card draw, and with no opposing creatures it would likely connect next turn.

message: Select an artifact card with mana cost {0} or {1}
annotation_description: Fetched a second Mox Opal when they already have one on the battlefield. Due to the legend rule, one immediately goes to the graveyard with no benefit, since Arcbound Ravager isn't on the battlefield yet to sacrifice it to. This wastes the powerful Urza's Saga tutor ability.

Casting Claws of Gix before Arcbound Ravager is suboptimal sequencing. With Mox Opal providing mana (metalcraft is active with Fiery Islet, Spirebluff Canal, and Mox Opal), they have exactly 2 mana available to cast Arcbound Ravager. By casting Claws of Gix first, they still get both down this turn since Claws costs 0, but the order matters: if they cast Ravager first, Ravager enters as a 1/1 (modular 1), then casting Claws of Gix triggers Ravager's... wait, Ravager doesn't have an artifact-enters trigger. However, the key consideration is that Claws of Gix is a 0-mana artifact that could be sacrificed to Ravager later regardless of when it's cast. The real issue is that casting Claws first doesn't help toward Kappa Cannoneer's improvise any more than casting Ravager first would. Actually, both get cast this turn either way. But casting Arcbound Ravager first is slightly better because it's the more impactful card - if the opponent has instant-speed interaction (like March of Wretched Sorrow), you'd rather have Ravager on board sooner to potentially sacrifice artifacts in response. More importantly, if they can only resolve one spell (e.g., opponent has a counterspell), Ravager is far more valuable than Claws of Gix. Claws of Gix provides minimal value in this board state.

chosen_display: Claws of Gix — {1}, Sacrifice a permanent: You gain 1 life. [Activate]
annotation_description: Sacrificing Mox Opal to Claws of Gix for 1 life is a significant waste of resources. Mox Opal is one of the most powerful mana-producing artifacts in Modern, and while metalcraft is currently off (only 2 artifacts remain: Claws of Gix and Mox Opal itself before sacrifice), the player has Arcbound Ravager in hand which would bring the artifact count back up. Playing Arcbound Ravager (2 artifacts on board + Ravager = 3 artifacts = metalcraft active) would re-enable Mox Opal as a mana source, which is critical for casting Kappa Cannoneer with improvise. At 11 life, gaining 1 life is negligible, while losing Mox Opal significantly reduces the ability to cast the Kappa Cannoneer (which needs 6 mana, reducible by tapping artifacts via improvise). Each artifact on board matters enormously for improvise and for Construct token sizing from any future Urza's Saga. The player threw away a key resource for virtually no benefit.

annotation_description: GPT4om Sarge is choosing the target for March of Wretched Sorrow, which is on the stack alongside Inquisition of Kozilek. March of Wretched Sorrow deals X damage to a target creature or planeswalker and gains X life. The only two creatures available are both GPT4om Sarge's own creatures (Orcish Bowmasters and Orc Army Token). Choosing to kill their own Orcish Bowmasters — a powerful 1/1 with a triggered ability that punishes opponent card draws — is terrible. If forced to target their own creature, the Orc Army Token (a 1/1 vanilla token) is far less valuable to sacrifice. However, the real question is why March of Wretched Sorrow is being cast at all when there are no enemy creatures or planeswalkers to target — it's being used to kill their own creature for no benefit beyond a small life gain, which is a waste of a card.

message: Select a nonland card with mana value 3 or less
annotation_description: Inquisition of Kozilek can only take nonland cards with mana value 3 or less. Kappa Cannoneer has mana value 6, so it cannot legally be chosen by Inquisition. Arcbound Ravager (mana value 2) is the only legal and correct choice. Beyond the legality issue, Arcbound Ravager is a strong threat in an artifact-based deck that enables explosive turns with sacrifice synergies, so taking it would have been the correct play regardless.

Sacrificing one of only two colored mana sources leaves them unable to cast Ravager this turn and severely constrains future mana development, making it much harder to eventually cast Kappa Cannoneer.

The only possible target is GPT4om Sarge's own Orc Army Token, which would be counterproductive - killing their own attacker. chosen_display: Fiery Islet — {1}, {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Draw a card. [Activate]
annotation_description: At 6 life, sacrificing Fiery Islet to draw a card costs 1 life (going to 5) and destroys a land, reducing mana availability for casting Kappa Cannoneer next turn. The player has Weapons Manufacturing in hand and could cast it with the available mana (Mox Opal + Fiery Islet for {1}{R}), or play Steam Vents as a land drop to set up for Kappa Cannoneer. Drawing a card is speculative when life is precious at 6 and the board position is already dire (opponent at 24). Losing the land also makes it harder to cast the 6-mana Kappa Cannoneers in hand. Playing Steam Vents (untapped, paying 2 life to go to 4) and casting Weapons Manufacturing would have been a more constructive line, building toward a board presence.

chosen_display: Castle Locthwain — {1}{B}{B}, {T}: Draw a card, then you lose life e... [Activate]
annotation_description: The opponent is at 3 life with all lands tapped. GPT4om Sarge has Thoughtseize in hand which costs {B} and would make the opponent reveal their hand, allowing selection of their best remaining card. Thoughtseize costs 2 life to the caster (bringing them to 22), but the opponent is at 3 life and has no untapped mana, so there's no risk. Instead, GPT4om Sarge activated Castle Locthwain to draw a card, which costs {1}{B}{B} and taps Castle Locthwain, using all available mana and preventing casting Thoughtseize this turn. Additionally, Castle Locthwain's draw causes life loss equal to cards in hand (currently 1 card in hand, so after drawing it becomes 2 cards, losing 2 life - same as Thoughtseize). More importantly, drawing a card triggers the opponent's potential Orcish Bowmasters if they have one, and the opponent has Weapons Manufacturing on the battlefield which could generate value. The key issue is that Thoughtseize would strip a key card from the opponent's hand (like Kappa Cannoneer or Arcbound Ravager which were revealed earlier), while drawing a random card is less impactful when you're already far ahead on life and the opponent is at 3. Casting Thoughtseize first to see their hand and strip their best threat is clearly better sequencing - you can always activate Castle Locthwain on a later turn.

chosen_display: Shadowspear — {1}: Permanents your opponents control lose hexpr... [Activate]
annotation_description: Qwen3L ESPN activated Shadowspear's ability to remove hexproof and indestructible from opponent's permanents, but the opponent has no permanents with hexproof or indestructible. This wastes 1 mana for no benefit. At 3 life with Kappa Cannoneer in hand needing 6 mana (with improvise helping), every mana matters. The mana spent on Shadowspear's ability could have been used toward casting Kappa Cannoneer or kept available for other plays.

chosen_display: Castle Locthwain — {1}{B}{B}, {T}: Draw a card, then you lose life e... [Activate]
annotation_description: Activated Castle Locthwain to draw before playing Polluted Delta from hand. With 0 cards in hand and the opponent at 2 life, the drawn card could require mana to cast. Playing Polluted Delta first (free land drop) would provide an additional mana source to potentially use whatever is drawn. The land drop is free and should always come before spending mana on draw effects.

At 2 HP, Kappa Cannoneer is a far superior play. It has Improvise to help cast it, enters as a 4/4 that immediately gets +1/+1 counters from its own ETB and Weapons Manufacturing triggers (creating Munitions tokens that trigger more counters). It's unblockable the turn it enters, making it a massive immediate threat that could be equipped with Shadowspear for lifelink to stabilize. Pinnacle Emissary as a 3/3 is much less impactful and doesn't pressure the opponent's 19 life nearly as effectively.
